lines.text: On time, driver. That's what I like to see.
A few minutes late tonight. Don't make it a habit.
You were late tonight, driver. Very late. People notice.
Evening, new driver. This is Rhee, night dispatch. You'll be hearing a lot of me.
Route 9 runs forty minutes, depot to Northgate. Two rules. You don't run late. And you don't let anyone ride free.
The cameras see everything. So do I.
End of the line.
Northgate, then.
If you say so.
You've got kind eyes. I've seen them before. That's going to make this harder for you.
You're exactly on schedule, driver. Let's keep it that way.
Thank you. Oh my god, thank you. I'm Mara. If I'm late one more time they'll take me off nights, and I can't afford days.
Good. That's how it's done.
St. Agnes. Twelve-hour shifts. You get used to the quiet. Mostly.
You're new. The last guy quit after a week. Said the bus was always cold. Said he kept hearing people in the back.
He was kind of a weirdo, though.
You know this route used to go farther? Past Northgate, out to Ashgrove. Before the bridge.
A storm took it out. Way before I was born. My mom says they never found all the—
Never mind. It's a sad story for a bus at midnight.
I don't... I don't have the fare. I just need to get to Northgate. Please. I'll pay you back tomorrow, I swear.
Reminder, driver. No. Free. Rides.
Thanks. I'm Jun. In case you need it for, like, a report.
I saw that, driver. That's your one warning.
Is he okay? The old guy in the back? He's not blinking.
This is me. St. Agnes.
Made it with a minute to spare. You're a lifesaver. Literally, probably. Same bus tomorrow?
Hey! That was my stop! Great. Now I'm walking back.
Don't slow down, driver. That stop isn't on the schedule.
I'll walk from here. Thanks for nothing.
Ashgrove, please.
This bus doesn't go to Ashgrove.
No. I suppose it doesn't. Not anymore.
Watch the road, driver. You're drifting.
Dispatch to Route 9. Northgate's clear tonight. Pull in, sign the log, and leave the keys in the—
What was that? What WAS that?
Eyes on the road, driver. You'll see all sorts of things on nights.
You stop a lot, driver. For a lot of people. Teodor used to stop for everyone.
Who's Teodor?
Nobody. A driver who ran late.
Not bad for a first night, driver. Keep your eyes on the clock, and off the mirror.
End of the line, huh. Thanks for the scenic route.
Thanks. Seriously. I'll pay you back.
End of the line, sir.
Not yet, it isn't.
Driver. Your display is malfunctioning. Ignore it.
Whatever it shows you. Ignore it.
You came back.
And no more free rides. I mean it.
Get some sleep. Same time tomorrow.
First night on Route 9. Nobody else wanted the shift.
I asked for it. I didn't tell them why.
There's an old man in the back row. I didn't see him get on.
Elm and Fourth is first. Then Market, St. Agnes, Canal Row, Northgate.
Someone's running for the bus. A nurse, I think. She's a long way back.
She stopped running. She's just standing under the streetlight. Watching me go.
Was someone running for the bus back there? Too late now.
She was looking past me. At the back row.
He nodded like he'd heard it before. It's six miles to Northgate.
There was a kid on the bench at Market. He watched the bus go by.
I don't look. I don't want to look.
Every window in the hospital is lit. Someone's standing in a window on the fourth floor.
There's someone at the old request stop. The one they took out of service years ago.
No. Not someone. It's like somebody cut the shape of a man out of the night.
Its head turned to follow me. Then the light went out. And it was gone.
Canal Row. The route sheet says nobody ever gets on here.
Nobody. Just water on the road. It hasn't rained all week.
He sat right behind me. I can hear him dripping.
He's staring at the back of my head.
He's gone. There's just a puddle on his seat, spreading.
A face, pressed against my window. On the inside.
Okay. Breathe. Northgate's not far now. Just drive the bus.
It hit the glass. It was on the glass, pressed flat, looking in at me. It doesn't have a face. It doesn't have anything.
It came down off the roof. How long was it up there? How long was it riding with me?
There are handprints on the windshield. On the outside. They're not wet. They're ash.
The route display. It's showing a stop after Northgate. There's nothing after Northgate.
He's gone. I didn't hear the doors. Something fell back there. I heard it hit the floor and roll. His seat is soaking wet.
I'm alone on the bus. I'm alone on the bus.
NIGHT ROUTE 9. DEPOT TO NORTHGATE. 11:40 PM.
DO NOT RUN LATE. NO FREE RIDES. DISPATCH IS WATCHING.
Someone's written underneath in pencil. Stop for them.
Sir? Where are you headed?
What happened to the bridge?
Sit down. This one's on me.
Sorry, kid. Rules.
Evening, driver. Northgate by twelve twenty. And your display is still broken, so don't look at it.
You saw it, then.
There was a stop past Northgate once. Ashgrove. Little houses by the river. Kids who'd wave at the bus.
The bridge went down in March of ninety-four. In a storm. With the last bus of the night on it.
Which route?
This one.
Dispatch, this is Route 9. The river's coming over the road at Canal. I want to hold at Northgate till it passes.
Negative, Nine. You're eleven minutes down. Make up the time.
Harold, I've got kids on this bus.
Then get them home on schedule.
Old tapes, driver. The system plays them back sometimes. Ignore it.
Figured I owe you a coffee. It's terrible. Hospital coffee always is.
Heads up. A water main burst on Canal Row. It's deep. Take it slow, or you'll stall out in the middle of it.
I got written up. One more and I'm off nights. So thanks for that.
Yeah. Okay. Everybody's got a schedule. I get it.
Canal Row's flooded tonight. Go slow or you'll stall in it.
There's a man on my ward. Room four B. Ninety-one years old. No visitors. Ever.
He barely talks. But every night, right around this time, he opens his eyes and asks me two things.
What time is it. And is Route 9 running yet.
I always tell him yes. It seems to help.
My mom was a nurse at St. Agnes back then too. She lost a friend on that bus. She never really talked about it.
I'm paying tonight. And here's yesterday's. Don't want you getting in trouble.
My mom cleans the Northgate depot. Nights. She works two jobs, so nights are kind of the only time I see her.
She gets off at twelve thirty. If I'm there before then, we walk home together.
Can I ask you something weird? Last night, when we got to Northgate. Did you count how many people got off?
Just you.
There were six people in the back when I got off. All wet. All looking at you.
Hello? Jun? Jun, is that you?
No, I'm sorry. I'm the Route 9 driver. I saw him last night at Market Street. He was trying to get to Northgate.
Northgate. He was coming to me. I work at the Northgate depot. He was walking to me.
Thank you. I'll call the police. Thank you.
Driver. Personal calls are not on the schedule.
Okay. I saw that. I definitely saw that.
You're drifting, driver. Eyes front.
Hey. Weird question. If you ever see a stop that isn't supposed to be there...
My mom used to say the drowned don't want to scare you. They just want a ride home.
Forget it. I'm tired. See you tomorrow.
Seriously? That was my stop.
The bridge is gone. It's been gone a long time.
This bus doesn't go there.
Everyone keeps telling me.
I'm Daniel. My daughter's Rosie. She turns six tonight. I promised her I'd be home before she fell asleep.
I think I'm very late.
You're kind. He was kind too. The driver.
He wanted to wait out the storm. But the man on the radio kept saying make up the time. Make up the time.
The man on the radio told him to make up the time. Did you know that? He wanted to wait.
Driver. Do NOT open those doors. They are not on the manifest.
It's not their night yet. But you could let them see you.
Not yet. Not tonight.
I'm Lena. You're the first one who's opened the doors in a very long time.
Have we met? You look so much like someone I
He's still riding, isn't he? Every night. Tell him we don't blame him. We never did.
Driver. Close. The. Doors.
Good. Good driver.
Night, driver.
Storm's coming in off the river tomorrow. A big one. Like the old days.
You'll want to make up the time.
I barely slept. Every time I closed my eyes I heard dripping.
Mom took the last bus home every night. That's most of what I remember about her. Her keys in the door, at one in the morning.
And then one night, the keys didn't come.
He's back. Same seat. Same wet shoes.
And the stop with no name moved. It's before Northgate now.
The old man in the back row is crying. He isn't making a sound.
Mara was at the stop. I didn't pick her up. Again.
The old man has his eyes closed. He might be smiling.
Jun was waiting with exact change. I left him there.
Something's moving on the sidewalk. Out of the corner of my eye. Keeping up with the bus.
The thing from the windshield. It ran beside the bus. I was doing thirty.
Too fast. The engine's drowned. It won't turn over.
Someone's knocking on the doors.
He's shivering so hard his teeth click.
Something wet is touching the back of my neck.
I'm not opening those doors.
Hands. All over the door glass. Gray and wrinkled from the water.
I can hear someone breathing. Somewhere behind me.
There's nothing there. There's nothing there. There's nothing there.
I'm slowing down. I'm not touching the brake.
There's a shelter where there's never been a shelter. Lit up yellow. It's raining inside it. Only inside it.
Nobody's getting on.
She stopped. She's looking at me like she knows me.
A little girl at the front of the shelter waved at the bus. The way kids used to wave at buses.
The back row is empty again. Something hit the floor back there and rolled. Another wet seat.
The display flickered. The stop with no name moved again. It's after St. Agnes now. It's getting closer.
NOTICE: DEPOT CAMERAS SHOW NO PASSENGERS BOARDING ROUTE 9 AT THE DEPOT.
I checked the tape before my shift. It shows me getting on alone.
There's a poster on the shelter. MISSING. Jun Park, fifteen. Last seen Market Street, around midnight.
It's the kid from last night. There's a phone number. Underneath, someone wrote: please. anything.
That stop on the display. What is it?
I'm sorry. I should have waited.
Why do you ride to Northgate every night?
The lights are back. He's gone. My jacket is folded on his seat. Soaked through. Still warm.
The lights are back. His seat is empty, and dark with water.
Two perfect nights, driver. Don't spoil it in the rain.
You're behind this week, driver. In weather like this, drivers make mistakes. Don't.
And I haven't forgotten about the free ride.
It's like the sky is falling. Thank you.
Can I ask you something, and you don't think I'm crazy? Mr. Varga, in four B. He's getting worse. Tonight or tomorrow, the doctors say.
He's stopped asking if Route 9 is running. Now he asks for the driver. The new driver. By name.
I never told him your name.
Would you come up? When we get to St. Agnes? Just for a minute. I think he's waiting for you.
Right. The schedule.
I almost didn't come. I didn't want to ride tonight. But Mom's working, and the trains are down.
Are they real? The people in the back? Please don't tell me I'm crazy.
Okay. Real. That's better than being crazy, actually.
They don't look mean. They look sad. Like when you wait for someone at the airport and they never come out.
You. You're the driver who called.
The police found him on the road to Northgate. Halfway there, in the dark. He was walking to me.
He's home. He's asleep in his bed right now. Because you called.
Repeating our top story. At twelve thirty-one this morning, the Ashgrove bridge collapsed during the storm.
A Route 9 city bus was crossing at the time. Divers have recovered fourteen.
The driver, Teodor Varga, fifty-eight, was pulled from the river alive, and is in critical condition at St. Agnes.
Among the dead, a St. Agnes nurse, Lena Marsh, thirty-one, who leaves behind a four-year-old child.
Dispatch records show the bus was running eleven minutes behind sched
That's enough of that.
Fourth floor. Room four B. Please.
Driver. You have no scheduled break at St. Agnes.
Okay. Okay. I'll tell him you're coming tomorrow.
CLOSE THE DOORS. Driver, CLOSE THEM.
She's in there, you know. Your mother. In the cardigan. She sat right behind me every night.
Is it time yet?
Not tonight, Ivy. Soon. I promise. Soon.
Can I sit up front? Mister Teodor always let me ring the bell.
That's my stop. That's always my stop.
You'll regret that, driver.
It's on the glass! It's ON the glass!
Keep driving, driver. You don't stop for weather.
This is me. Jun wants to meet you, you know. The driver who called. He thinks you're some kind of hero.
Ignore that.
This way. Fourth floor smells like bleach and old flowers. You stop noticing.
He hasn't moved in three days.
You came back. Lena's child. You came back for her.
Don't let him make you late.
The man on the radio. Don't listen to him. He told me to make up the time, and I listened.
Fourteen. I listened, and it was fourteen.
He's been waiting thirty years for somebody to stop.
The rain is so loud on the depot roof it sounds like applause.
My jacket is hanging behind the driver's seat. I left it soaked on Canal Row. It's dry now. It smells like the river.
He's back there again. He looks worse tonight. Grayer. Like a photo left in the sun.
Mara was waiting in the rain. I didn't stop.
Nobody's here. Someone left a nurse's lanyard hanging on the shelter. It's swinging in the wind.
The poster's pulped by the rain. Someone has put up two more.
There's a kid with a huge backpack in the back row.
Nobody. It was nobody.
Lena Marsh.
My mother's name was Lena Marsh. I was four.
The woman in the shelter. Lena. She looked at me like she knew me. Because she did.
Nobody ever told me how. They just said there was an accident. They just said she wasn't coming home.
Varga. Teodor Varga. He's looking at the radio. Then at me. He nods. Very slightly.
Up on the fourth floor, a thin figure is pressing one hand against the window glass.
The doors opened by themselves.
Knocking. Not on the doors. Under the floor. Under my feet. Like people trapped in something, beating on the walls.
She's looking right at me. She's soaking wet. She's younger than I am now.
She's gone. The seat is soaking wet. There's a tiny yellow button on it.
Hands. On every window of the bus. Gray. Wrinkled. Pressing.
I don't feel like a good driver.
Canal Row is a river now. The water's up to the second step.
In the lightning, there are faces under the water. Looking up.
Every time the lightning goes, the whole road lights up for a second.
There's something standing in the road.
It's back. The thing from the first night. Spread across the glass like it's trying to get in.
Then the lights went, and it was gone. Only the handprints stayed. The rain won't wash them off.
There's a sheet of paper under my windshield wiper.
The stop with no name moved again. It's right after Market Street now.
It's him. The old man from the back row. Same hands. Same wet-looking eyes. Tubes in his arm.
My bus is down there in the rain. And someone's sitting in the back row. Looking up at me.
His hand let go. The monitor keeps counting. Slow.
The missing poster has a strip pasted across it. FOUND SAFE.
Notice. Route 9 radio moves to channel 4 starting tomorrow. Channel 9 has been out of service since nineteen ninety-four. Dana, night dispatch.
I'll try.
I don't get breaks on Route 9.
They're real. Sit up front with me. You're safe up here.
It's just the storm. Sit down.
Just for a minute. Go ahead.
Thanks for believing me.
Night. Be careful, okay?
Route 9? Route 9, is that you? Oh thank god. This is Dana, night dispatch.
Where have you been all week? We've had zero contact from your bus. Your GPS keeps dropping out at a spot that isn't on any map.
I've been checking in every night. With Rhee. Night dispatch.
Rhee?
Harold Rhee was dispatch here in the nineties. He ran Route 9 the night the bridge went down.
He died in ninety-five. After the inquiry. They found him in the dispatch office with the radio still on.
Hello, Dana.

You don't need channel 4, driver. You've got me.
That doesn't work, driver.
It didn't work for Teodor either.
I'm not riding. I'm walking in. It's Mr. Varga. They think it's tonight. Maybe tomorrow.
He woke up for about a minute after you left. He said, give this to the driver.
He keeps saying fourteen. Just the number. Over and over.
I'll be with him. He won't be alone. I promise.
Put that away, driver. Teodor kept that for thirty years. Look where it got him.
From my mom. Soup. She says you look like you don't eat.
Don't go past Market tonight. Please. I had a dream. The bus was in the river, and you were driving, and all the windows were full of faces.
Just. If something tells you to go faster? Don't.
You grew up.
Don't look at me, sweetheart. Look at the road. He's going to make you drive.
There we go. Full bus. Just like the old days.
You're eleven minutes late, driver.
MAKE UP THE TIME.
Faster. FASTER. The schedule always comes first.
You said that to him too.
He stopped. He stopped this time.
That's my kid. That's my kid.
GOOD. GOOD DRIVER.
No. No, no, no. Not you too.
That's how it's done. You'll do it properly next time.
Route 9, if you can hear this, it's Dana. Don't answer. Just listen.
I pulled Harold Rhee's file. After the inquiry he never went home. He slept in the dispatch office.
Every night at twelve nineteen he read out the Route 9 stops on channel 9. To nobody. Elm and Fourth. Market. St. Agnes. Canal Row. Northgate. Ashgrove.
The night he died, he got as far as Ashgrove and stopped. Like he couldn't say what came after.
That's enough, Dana.
Eyes front, driver. You've got a schedule to keep.
Route 9! Route 9, come in. Your bus went dark for six minutes. GPS put you in the middle of the river. Are you okay?
I'm okay. I think.
Listen to me. Whatever you're hearing on channel 9, it isn't us. Nobody's been on that channel since
Since me.
Tomorrow's the last run, driver. The stop is coming to you.
The back row is empty tonight. Just a dark stain on the seat that never dries.
The radio is off. The light is off. His voice is still coming out of it.
A brass name badge. The pin's bent. The letters are worn soft by a thumb. T. Varga. Route 9.
The bus coughed and rolled to a stop on its own. The engine's still running.
A streetlight glare, right in my eyes.
Something fell out of the visor into my lap. A newspaper clipping, folded small. Someone kept it a long time.
The posters are gone. Washed off, or torn down. There's a soaked backpack on the bench nobody's claimed.
The doors opened by themselves. This time they don't wait for me. They're getting on.
Fourteen. They don't pay. They don't look at me. They sit, and they drip.
Water. Around my shoes. Rising.
Someone sat down right behind me. I can feel cold coming off her, like an open freezer.
Mom.
I'm not. The clock says I'm not.
The pedal is going down by itself.
The street's gone. The buildings are gone. The road is getting narrower.
Under the last streetlight. The shadow. It's pointing at the bridge.
It stopped. The front wheels are on the last slab of the bridge. Under me there's nothing. Just the river, waiting.
Behind me, fourteen people let out a breath they've been holding for thirty years.
I'm parked outside St. Agnes. The bus is bone dry. My clothes are soaked through. I can taste the river.
I'm parked outside St. Agnes. The bus is dry. The engine ticks as it cools.
Up on the fourth floor, the window of four B is lit. Dimmer now. The thin figure is holding up one finger.
One more night.
Someone's standing at the back of the bus. I can see them in the mirror.
Nobody. Nothing. But the air back here smells like a struck match.
The stop with no name is right after Elm and Fourth now. Tomorrow, it'll be waiting.
Inquiry. Dispatcher ordered bus onto bridge.
Route 9 driver Teodor Varga radioed dispatch at twelve nineteen, asking permission to wait out the storm at Northgate.
Dispatcher Harold Rhee refused. Recordings show Rhee told Varga, eleven minutes behind schedule, to make up the time by taking the Ashgrove bridge.
Asked if he regretted the order, Rhee said: the schedule always comes first. That's the job.
There's a photo of the victims. Fourteen faces. A woman in a cardigan, holding a little kid on her hip.
The kid is me.
Under the article, in shaky pencil, one word, over and over, until the paper tore. Stop. Stop. Stop. Stop.
There's a little box on the dashboard, wrapped in soggy paper with balloons on it. For Rosie. Love, Dad.
Underneath, newer, in shaky handwriting: she waits at Elm and Fourth. She doesn't know why.
Last run, driver. Big night. Full bus.
You know what to do. You make up the time.
Sorry. I'm not riding. I just come here. Every year, on this night. I don't even really know why.
My dad took the last bus home on this night. I was six. It was my birthday. He promised he'd be home before I fell asleep.
I stayed awake all night. I'm Rosie, by the way. Sorry. You don't need my life story.
That's his handwriting.
He remembered. He got it for me. He was bringing it home.
How do you know his name?
He rides this bus. He talks about you. He was bringing you a present.
I always felt like he was trying. Like he was out there, still trying to get home.
March fourteenth, nineteen ninety-four. I was eleven minutes late.
I asked to wait out the storm. Harold said no. Harold said make up the time. And I was scared of losing my job, and I had a schedule, and I did what I was told.
Fourteen people. Lena. Daniel. Little Ivy. Eleven more. I knew every one of their faces. I used to wave.
Your mother sat right behind me, every night. She talked about her kid the whole way home. You. She talked about you.
They pulled me out of the river alive. Everyone said I survived.
I didn't. I've been riding this bus every night since. Waiting for a driver who would stop.
Right now there's a nurse holding my hand in Room four B. She's very kind. She tells me Route 9 is running.
It's my last night too. Tonight they get on, or they never do.
Stop for them. That's all. That's all it ever was. Stop for people.
Because you stop. I've watched you all week. You stop for people when it costs you.
Because you're who's driving. And because I'm out of nights.
Don't listen to him, driver. He's the one who drowned them.
Hi, sweetheart.
DRIVER.

The schedule ALWAYS comes first. That's the JOB.
Please.
DON'T YOU

Thank you for stopping.

Everyone gets a ride home. That's the job.

I missed you.
I know. I was always on my way back. Always.
Mind if I drive the last bit?
Route 9, this is Dana on channel 4. You okay? I've got you back on GPS. Clean signal for the first time all week.

We'll know when you are.
Not yet, sweetheart. Not yet.
Tomorrow, then. And the night after. As long as it takes.
Good. GOOD. Back on schedule.
You didn't stop.
Evening, driver. See you tomorrow night.
And the night after that.
Last night. I reached into my pocket for my keys and found coins instead. Four of them. Heavy. Worn smooth.
And the brass badge. T. Varga. It's warm, like someone was just holding it.
Thirty-two years. Tonight I find out if she ever gets home.
The stain on the back seat has spread across three seats now.
Two people at Elm and Fourth. A woman on the bench. And a man under the streetlight in an old brown driver's uniform.
Her hands are shaking so much I have to help her with the paper. Inside is a music box. Cheap. Painted. A little dancer with a chipped arm.
It's playing the same notes I've been hearing in my head all week.
The man in the uniform took off his cap. He's getting on.
The display stopped flickering. For the first time, the stop has a name. Ashgrove.
Fourteen of them. Standing in a rain that isn't falling anywhere else. They're not knocking. They're just waiting. Like they always have.
And between them and my doors, the shadow. Arms out. Keeping them off my bus. It's been keeping them off for thirty-two years.
The shadow at the doors is coming apart. Like smoke. Like it was only ever his voice.
Dead air. It's the best sound I've ever heard.
Someone's crying in the back row. A thin, gray man in a dispatcher's cardigan, with a headset around his neck.
The shadow stepped back from the doors. Just one step. Enough to let them through. It's still watching.
For a moment, nobody moves. Then Daniel climbs the steps. He isn't dripping anymore.
Fourteen fares. Fourteen old coins in the box. Ivy rang the bell and giggled.
He drives like he never left. The road ends. The bridge isn't there anymore. We just keep going.
Below us, the river is full of stars.
Northgate. Morning. The bus is empty, and dry.
For the first time in thirty-two years, I think she made it home.
Somewhere across town, a music box is playing on a kitchen table. And a woman is finally asleep.
Jun is here with two coffees. He doesn't say anything. He just hands me one.

Nobody moves.

Ashgrove is still on my route display when I clock out. It'll be there tomorrow, too.
Every seat is full. Fourteen people, soaked to the bone, staring straight ahead.
Mom is in the seat right behind me.
Water is creeping across the floor. I can't feel my feet.
Northgate. The clock on the dash settles on twelve twenty. Exactly on time.
My hands on the wheel are gray. Wrinkled. Like they've been underwater for a very long time.

Why me?
Your dad's name was Daniel. He was trying to get home to you.
